6.54.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / What is the name of the eleventh day in the bright half of Śrāvaṇa? / Tell that to us, O Govinda, O Vāsudeva! Praise be to you!
The venerable Kṛṣṇa said: / Listen, O king; I will tell you the sin-destroying account / which was formerly spoken by Brahmā to Nārada when he inquired.
Nārada said: / O Blessed One, born on the lotus, I desire to hear from you: / What is the name of the eleventh day in the dark half of Śrāvaṇa?
Who is its deity, what is its procedure, and what is its merit? Tell me, O Lord! / Hearing his words, Brahmā spoke these words.
Brahmā said: / Listen, O Nārada; wishing for the welfare of the worlds, I tell you: / The dark eleventh day of Śrāvaṇa is celebrated by the name of Kāmikā.
Merely by hearing of it, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. / On it, whoever worships the Lord of gods, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace,
Hari, Viṣṇu, Mādhava, Madhusūdana, named Śrīdhara— / whoever indeed worships and meditates on him, hear his meritorious fruit:
Neither at the Gaṅgā, nor in Kāśī, nor in Naimiṣa, nor in Puṣkara / does one obtain that fruit which is obtained from the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever fruit one obtains at the Godāvarī when Jupiter is in Leo, at Vyatīpāta, and in Daṇḍaka, / that fruit one obtains from the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
One who gives the earth together with its oceans and forests, / and one who performs the vow of Kāmikā—both are remembered as having equal fruit.
A man who gives a cow that is calving along with all its accessories / obtains that [same] fruit by performing the vow of Kāmikā.
Whatever best of men worships the god Śrīdhara in Śrāvaṇa, / by him alone are the gods, Gandharvas, Urugas, and Pannagas worshipped.
Therefore, on the day of Kāmikā, Hari must be worshipped with every effort / by mortals fearing sin, according to their ability.
For those who are sunk in the ocean of worldly existence filled with the mire of sin, / the excellent vow of Kāmikā exists for the sake of their deliverance.
There is nothing higher than this, purifying and removing sin; / know it thus, O Nārada: supreme Hari has said so himself.
Know that the fruit of those who practice the vow of Kāmikā / is far greater than what is obtained by men dedicated to the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
The man who performs the vow of Kāmikā, having kept an all-night vigil, / does not behold the terrible Yama, nor does he go to a miserable state.
Nor does he see an evil birth, because of observing the vow of Kāmikā. / When the vow of Kāmikā was observed, yogins attained isolation.
Therefore, it should be performed with every effort by those whose minds are restrained. / The man who worships Hari with leaves grown from the tulasī plant,
is not smeared with sin, just as a lotus leaf [is not smeared] with water. / A bhāra of gold and four times as much silver—
he attains that fruit from worship with a tulasī leaf. / Viṣṇu, worshipped with gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, corals, and the like,

is not so pleased as he is with a sprig of tulasī. / And one by whom Keśava has been worshipped with tulasī blossoms—

Who, when seen, pacifies the multitude of all sins; when touched, purifies the body; / when praised, drives away diseases; and when sprinkled [with water], terrifies Death:
when planted, brings about nearness to the blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa; / when laid at his feet, bestows the fruit of liberation—to that Tulasī, homage!
The mortal who gives a lamp day and night on the day of Hari— / Citragupta is not at all able to calculate his merit.
One whose lamp burns before Kṛṣṇa on the day of the eleventh, / his ancestors resting in heaven are satisfied with nectar.
Having lit a lamp with ghee or again with sesame oil, / he travels to the world of the sun, honored with hundreds of millions of lamps.
This glory of Kāmikā has been described by me before you; / therefore, it must be performed by men, taking away all fallen deeds,
removing the murder of a brahmin, destroying the killing of an embryo, / giving a place with Viṣṇu, and bestowing the fruit of great merit.
Having heard this glorification endowed with faith, a man / attains the world of Viṣṇu and is completely freed from all sins.

6.55.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / What is the name of the eleventh day in the bright half of Śrāvaṇa? / By your grace, speak before me, O Madhusūdana!
The venerable Kṛṣṇa said: / Listen attentively, O king, to the supreme tale that takes away sin, / merely by the hearing of which there is the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Dvāpara age, in the city of Māhiṣmatī, / a king named Mahījit was ruling his kingdom.
Because he was childless, that kingdom brought him no happiness. / For a sonless man there is no happiness, in this world or in the next.
Much time passed for him thus in anxiety over a son, / and a son, who gives all joy to men, was not obtained by the king.
Seeing himself advanced in years, the king became filled with worry. / Then, having gone into the midst of his subjects, he spoke these words:
'In this birth, O people, no wickedness has been done by me; / wealth acquired unjustly was not deposited in the treasury by me.

The property of brahmins or the wealth of gods was never taken by me anywhere; / no appropriation of another's trust, which produces great sin, was committed; / the subjects were protected like sons, and the earth was conquered through righteousness.'
'Punishment has been inflicted upon the wicked, even when equal to kinsmen or sons; / but the virtuous have ever been honoured, and no people are hated by me.'
“O best of the twice-born, while I profess such a righteous path, / why has no son been born in my house? Let that be considered!”
Hearing this speech, the twice-born, along with the subjects and the family priests, / took counsel for the king's welfare and went into the dense forest.
Looking here and there at the hermitages frequented by ṛṣis, / seeking the king's welfare, they saw an excellent sage,
performing severe penance, without support, free from ailment, / taking no food, self-controlled, having conquered anger, eternal,
Lomaśa, knower of the truth of dharma, skilled in all scriptures, / long-lived, great-souled, endowed with hair, equal to Brahmā.
With the passing of each kalpa, one hair of his falls out; / therefore this great sage, knower of the three divisions of time, is named Lomaśa.
Seeing him, all rejoiced and approached his presence; / according to rule and merit, they made their salutation as prescribed.

Bowed down with humility, they all said to one another: / 'Only through the power of our good fortune has this best of sages been found!' / Beholding them accompanied by the subjects, the best of ṛṣis spoke.

Lomaśa said:
For what purpose have you arrived here? Tell me the reason. / With glad minds from the sight [of me], why are you praising me?
Without doubt I shall do whatever brings you welfare. / The birth of people like me is for doing good to others, without doubt.

The people said:
Listen, we shall tell the reason for our coming; / we have come to your presence to cut off our doubt.
Other than the lotus-born [Brahmā], there is none superior to you or more exalted. / Therefore, driven by our task, we have approached your presence.
This king named Mahījit is at present without a son. / We are his subjects, O brāhmaṇa, protected by him like sons.
Seeing him bereft of a son, afflicted with sorrow through his sorrow, / we have come here to perform penance, having formed a firm resolve.
By his good fortune you have indeed been seen by us, O best of the twice-born; / solely by the sight of the great does success in undertakings occur for men.
Declare instruction, O sage, so that a son may be born to the king. / Hearing their words, the sage remained in meditation for a moment; / having known his former birth, the sage replied.

Lomaśa said:
In a former birth he was a vaiśya, devoid of wealth, a doer of cruel deeds, / intent on commercial activities, wandering from village to village.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, in the bright fortnight, on the tenth day, / when the sun had reached the middle of the sky, he arrived at a reservoir on the village boundary.
Seeing a small well containing water, he set his mind on drinking water. / Just then, a cow with her calf arrived there.
Afflicted by thirst, distressed by the summer heat, she drank water there; / driving away the drinking cow, he drank the water himself.
Through that sinful act, the king has become sonless; / through the merit of some birth, a kingdom free from thorns was obtained.
Tell of meritorious instruction by which the destruction of sin may occur, / so that by your favour a son may be born to the lord of the earth.

Lomaśa said:
In the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, there is the famous ekādaśī / named Putradā, granting desires; perform that vow, O people!
Having heard this and bowed down to the sage, they went to the city and observed the vow / according to rule and according to right, accompanied by a vigil.
Its completely spotless merit was given to the king by the people; / the merit being given, that queen conceived a handsome child.
When the time of delivery arrived, she gave birth to a vigorous son. / In the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun stands in Cancer,
on the twelfth lunar day, the investiture with the sacred thread for Vāsudeva is prescribed: / with threads of gold, silver, copper, linen, silk, or lotus fibres,
with kuśa grass, kāśa grass, and auspicious cotton spun by a brāhmaṇa woman. / Having bathed, one should purify the triple-twisted thread by tripling it.
The preliminary consecration [takes place] on the previous day at the time interval of cow-milking. / Having bowed to the Brahmins and having saluted the feet of the guru,
one should then keep vigil amidst the auspicious sound of songs. / Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Bhillas, and likewise Śūdras,
all established in their own duty, should make the sacred thread with devotion. / Then one should offer the sacred thread to the guru according to the rules.
One should worship Brahmins and Vaiṣṇavas with perfumes, flowers, and the like. / A twice-born should offer it to Viṣṇu with the mantra beginning with ‘Ato devā’.
A Śūdra, however, [should offer it] with the root mantra; as unto Viṣṇu, so unto Śiva. / The investiture of the sacred thread must be performed year after year by men
who desire enjoyment and liberation in the ocean of sorrow of worldly existence. / But whoever does not perform the investiture of the sacred thread according to rule,

that Vaiṣṇava's annual worship is entirely fruitless. / Hearing the glorification of this, a man is freed from sin; / having obtained the happiness of sons in this world, he goes to heaven in the next.

6.56.m:
Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses,

in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the dialogue between the husband of Umā and Nārada, the fifty-fifth chapter, named ‘The investiture of the sacred thread of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa and the Putradā Ekādaśī’.

6.57.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / What, indeed, is the name of the Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of Bhādra? / I wish to hear this; tell me, O Janārdana.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / In the bright fortnight of Nabhasya, what would be the name of the Ekādaśī? / Which is the deity, what is its procedure? Tell this to me, O Keśava.

6.58.m: Nārada said: / Speak out of your grace, O Four-faced One, homage to you! / In the bright fortnight of Nabhasya, what would be the name of the Ekādaśī? / I wish to hear this for the sake of worshipping Viṣṇu.
I shall tell before you an auspicious, ancient tale, / by the mere hearing of which a great sin is destroyed.
It bestows enjoyment and liberation, and grants happiness to people; / from reading it and hearing it, O king, one is freed from all sins.

6.59.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / "Tell me graciously, O Madhusūdana: / what is the name of the Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina?"

6.60.m:
The king said: / "Explain to me graciously, O venerable one, the Indirā observance: / by what rite is it to be performed, and in which fortnight and lunar day?"

Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Speak out of grace, in front of me, O Madhusūdana: / In the bright fortnight of Iṣa, what is the name of the Ekādaśī?
The Blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / Let it be heard, O tiger among kings; I shall speak in your presence: / In the dark fortnight of Kārttika, there is the very beautiful Ramā,
declared to be an Ekādaśī that removes great sins, supreme. / In connection with this, O king, I shall tell you its glorification.
In ancient times there was a king known as Mucukunda; / he had friendship with the king of gods, O king,
and had friendship in every way with Yama, Varuṇa, / Kubera, and also Bibhīṣaṇa, O king.
A devotee of Viṣṇu, true to his word, he was an exalted king. / While he was thus ruling the kingdom with all thorns eradicated, O king,
there was born in his house a daughter, Candrabhāgā, the best of rivers [by name]; / and she was given in marriage to Śobhana, the son of Candrasena.
Once he came to his father-in-law's house, O king; / and the day of the Ekādaśī observance arrived, granting great merit.
When the day of the vow arrived, Candrabhāgā thought: / 'What will happen, O lord of gods? My husband is extremely weak;
he cannot endure hunger, and my father's command is severe: / when the tenth day arrives, his drum is beaten [announcing]:
"One must not eat, one must not eat, one must not eat on the day of Hari!"' / Hearing the sound of the drum, Śobhana said to his beloved:
'What should I do, my darling? Give me counsel, O fair-faced one!' / Candrabhāgā said: / 'In my father's house, O lord, no one may eat today;
even by elephants, horses, young elephants, and other animals / grass, grain, and water must not be consumed on the day of Hari.
How, then, could human beings eat on the day of Hari, my dear? / If you eat, my beloved, you will incur censure.
Reflecting thus in your mind, make your resolve very firm.' / Śobhana said: 'True is this word, my love; I will observe the fast.
Whatever is ordained by destiny will indeed happen.' / Having thus made a firm resolve, he undertook the observance for the vow.
With his body tormented by hunger, he became extremely distressed. / While he was pondering thus, the sun sank down the mountain.
That night brought increasing joy to Vaiṣṇava men / devoted to the worship of Hari, whose minds were attached to the vigil.
It brought great suffering to Śobhana, O tiger among kings; / at the hour of sunrise, Śobhana met his death.
The king had him cremated with woods fit for royalty; / Candrabhāgā did not burn her own body along with her husband.
Having performed his funeral rites, she remained in her father's home; / and Śobhana, O best of kings, by the power of the Ramā vow,
reached a delightful celestial city upon a peak of Mount Mandara, / unsurpassed, unassailable, endowed with countless virtues,
with mansions made of golden pillars, adorned with jewels and lapis lazuli, / crystal, of diverse shapes, and splendidly beautified.
Seated upon a throne, with an auspicious white parasol and fly-whisks, / crowned and wearing earrings, adorned with necklaces and armlets, / praised by gandharvas and attended by hosts of apsarases,
there Śobhana shines forth like a second king of kings. / A man renowned as Somaśarman lived in the city of Mucukunda;
wandering in the course of a pilgrimage, the brāhmaṇa saw him. / Recognising him as the king's son-in-law, he approached him.
Śobhana too, realising that Somaśarman had arrived, / quickly rose from his seat and bowed to the best of brāhmaṇas.
He inquired about the welfare of his father-in-law, the king, / of his beloved Candrabhāgā, and likewise of the city.

Somaśarman said:
“All is well, O king, in your father-in-law's house; / Candrabhāgā is well, and all is well throughout the city.
Tell your own story, O king; this is a wondrous marvel! / A city so wondrous and lovely has never been seen anywhere by anyone.

Explain this, O lord of men: whence was this attained by you?”
Śobhana said:
“In the dark fortnight of Kārtika, the Ekādaśī named Ramā—
by fasting on that [day], O chief of brāhmaṇas, this impermanent city was attained by me. / O best of brāhmaṇas, act so that it becomes permanent.”

The brāhmaṇa said:
“How is it impermanent, and how indeed may it become permanent? / Tell me the truth, O king of kings; I will do it, not otherwise.”

Śobhana said:
“O brāhmaṇa, this supreme vow was performed by me devoid of faith; / therefore I consider it impermanent. Hear how it may become permanent:
Mucukunda's daughter is the most beautiful Candrabhāgā; / relate this matter to her, and it will become permanent.”

Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard his words, the brāhmaṇa went to Mucukunda's city / and related the whole matter in the presence of Candrabhāgā.
I saw his unassailable city, equal to Indra's; / he said it is impermanent. Act so that it becomes permanent.”

Candrabhāgā said:
“Take me there, O brāhmaṇa sage, eager as I am to see my husband; / by the merit of my own vow, I shall make the city permanent.
O brāhmaṇa, bring about our reunion; / for great merit is gained by uniting two who are separated.”
Having heard this, Somaśarman went along with her / to the hermitage of Vāmadeva near Mount Mandara.
Vāmadeva heard the whole account told by both of them; / he then consecrated the radiant Candrabhāgā with Vedic mantras.
By the power of the sage's mantras and by observing the day of Viṣṇu, / she obtained a celestial body and attained a celestial state.
She went near her husband, her eyes blooming with immense joy; / Śobhana was exceedingly rejoiced to see his beloved arrive.
Calling her close, he seated her on his left side; / then from joy Candrabhāgā spoke dear words to her beloved:
“Hear, my beloved, beneficial words concerning the merit that is in me. / From the time I exceeded eight years of age in my father's house,
ever since then, whatever Ekādaśī vow was performed by me / according to the prescribed rules, with a mind full of faith— / by the power of that merit, the city will become permanent,
and abound in all desires until the dissolution of beings.” / Thus, O tiger among kings, she delights together with her husband,
enjoying celestial pleasures, having a celestial form, and adorned with celestial ornaments; / and Śobhana too, of celestial body, delights along with her,
by the power of the Ramā vow, on the peak of Mount Mandara. / Indeed, like a wish-granting gem or like a wish-fulfilling cow
is this [vow] named Ramā, O king, which has been related to you by me; / its entire glorification has been heard by you, O sinless king.
The glorification that destroys sins has been recounted by me before you; / and concerning the Ekādaśī vows in both fortnights,
just as the dark [fortnight], so also the bright—one should make no distinction at all. / Observed, Ekādaśī bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation to men.
Just as a white cow or a black cow yields the same milk, / even so the two Ekādaśīs are traditionally held to give equal fruits.
That person who hears the glorification of the Ekādaśī vows / is freed from all sins and honored in the realm of Viṣṇu.

6.61.m:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
“The glorification of Ramā has been heard from you accurately, O Kṛṣṇa; / tell me, O honor-giver, about the one that occurs in the bright fortnight of Kārtika.”

The venerable Kṛṣṇa said:
“Hear, O king, I shall declare that which occurs in the bright half of Ūrja, / as it was told to Nārada by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.”

Nārada said:
“Tell me in detail the glorification of Prabodhinī, / on which Govinda, the instigator of virtuous deeds, awakens.”

Brahmā said:
“Listen, O best of sages, to the glorification of Prabodhinī, which destroys sins, / increases merit, and grants liberation to those of good intellect.
Sacred bathing places and lakes extending to the ocean roar only so long / as the Prabodhinī lunar day of Viṣṇu in Kārtika has not arrived.
The Gaṅgā and the Bhāgīrathī roar upon earth, O chief of brāhmaṇas, only so long / as the sin-destroying Haribodhinī in Kārtika has not arrived.
A thousand horse sacrifices and a hundred royal consecration sacrifices / a person obtains by just a single fast on Prabodhinī.
Whatever is difficult to obtain, whatever cannot be reached, whatever lies beyond the scope of the three worlds— / even that, unasked, Haribodhinī gives, [like] a son.
Sovereignty, wealth, wisdom, kingship, and fortunes of happiness / Haribodhinī gives to people when fasted upon with devotion.
Whatever sins are mentioned, as vast as Meru and Mandara, / the sin-destroyer burns away by just a single fast.
Whatever sin has been accumulated across thousands of previous lives, / a nocturnal vigil on this [day] burns it away like a heap of cotton.
He who fasts on Prabodhinī in accordance with his nature, / duly according to rule, O tiger among sages, obtains the stated fruit.
Whatever good deed a man performs according to the rules as enjoined, / though small, O best among sages, its fruit becomes equal to Meru.
But if one should perform a good deed devoid of rules, even as vast as Meru, / he obtains only an atom-sized fruit of that righteous act, O Nārada.
Those who meditate with mental concentration, those who will observe Bodhinī— / their ancestors dwell delighted in the world of Viṣṇu.”
Freed from hellish sufferings, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. / Even if a man has committed a terrible sin, such as killing a brahmin,
by keeping vigil for Viṣṇu, he becomes cleansed of sin. / The reward which is difficult to attain by sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice, O brahmin,
is obtained quite easily during the vigil of Prabodhinī. / Having bathed at all holy places, having given gold and the earth,
one obtains that [same] fruit which is gained by keeping vigil for Hari. / He alone is truly virtuous; his family alone is purified,
by whom Prabodhinī is observed in the month of Kārtika, O tiger among sages! / Just as death is certain for mortals, so wealth and the body are impermanent;
Knowing this, O best of sages, the day of Viṣṇu should be observed; / whatever sacred bathing places exist in the three worlds,
all of them reside in the house of him who observes Prabodhinī. / What need has he of many merits, by whom Prabodhinī is observed?
For this Haribodhinī in Kārtika grants sons and grandsons. / He is a man of knowledge, he is a yogi, he is an ascetic with subdued senses,
and enjoyment and liberation belong to him who worships [on] Haribodhinī. / Indeed, this [day] is dearest to Viṣṇu, an ally to the essence of dharma.
The man who observes it with devotion becomes an enjoyer of worldly pleasures. / Having fasted on Prabodhinī, a man does not enter a womb again.
Therefore, O Nārada, setting aside all [other] religious duties, one should perform it. / Whatever sin has been accumulated by deed, thought, or word,
Govinda washes away on the vigil of Prabodhinī. / Bathing, giving gifts, chanting prayers, and worship dedicated to Janārdana—
whatever a man performs on Prabodhinī, dear one, becomes imperishable. / The men who worship the divine Mādhava on that day with devotion,
fasting completely, are delivered from sins born of a hundred lifetimes. / This is a great vow, my son, destroying the multitude of great sins.
One should fast properly on Viṣṇu’s day of awakening. / Having pleased the Lord of the gods, Janārdana, through this vow,
illuminating all the directions, one goes to the abode of Hari. / It should be observed with effort by men desiring splendor and wealth.
Sin accumulated in childhood, in youth, and in old age, / sin committed over a hundred lifetimes, whether small or great—
Govinda washes it away when worshipped by men on this [day]. / Bringing wealth and grain, holy, the supreme remover of all sins,
having fasted on it with devotion to Hari, nothing ever remains unattainable. / The merit that is celebrated during an eclipse of the moon and sun,
is said to be multiplied a thousandfold in the vigil on Prabodhinī. / Bathing, charity, recitation of mantras, offerings in fire, study of the scriptures, worship of Hari—
all of that is multiplied ten million times when performed on Prabodhinī. / Whatever merit has been acquired by a man since birth,
all of that becomes useless if he does not observe the vow in Kārtika. / A man who passes Kārtika without observing a restriction for Viṣṇu
does not obtain the fruit of the merit acquired throughout his life, O Nārada. / Therefore, with all effort, one should attend upon the God of gods, Janārdana,
who grants the fruit of all desires, O chief of brahmins. / He who, devoted to Viṣṇu, avoids another’s food during Kārtika,
by avoiding another's food, dear one, obtains the fruit of a cāndrāyaṇa penance. / Daily taking delight in sacred texts during Kārtika, Madhusūdana
burns away all his sins, and he obtains the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices. / Madhusūdana is not as pleased by sacrifices, by charity, or by prayers and the like,
as he is by discourses on the scriptures in the month of Kārtika. / Those who relate Viṣṇu’s tales, and those endowed with goodness who listen,
even to half a verse or a quarter of a verse in Kārtika, [attain] the fruit of a hundred cows. / Setting aside all [other] religious duties, in front of Keśava in Kārtika,
one should retain the sacred scriptures and listen to them, O great sage. / He who narrates Hari’s story desiring supreme welfare,
in the month of Kārtika, O tiger among sages, delivers a hundred families. / That man who listens to a narrative of Viṣṇu according to rule,
especially in Kārtika, obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. / He who listens to a narrative of Hari on Viṣṇu’s day of awakening,
attains the reward of giving the earth with its seven continents, O sage. / Having heard the divine tale of Viṣṇu, those who worship the narrator,
according to their means, O tiger among sages, their world is remembered as imperishable. / The man who passes Kārtika with the enjoyment of song and sacred learning,
has no rebirth; this has been seen by me, O lover of strife! / Song, dance, instrumental music, and auspicious tales of Viṣṇu, O sage—
whoever performs these is a virtuous soul residing above the three worlds. / With many flowers, many fruits, with camphor, aloe-wood, and saffron,
worship of Hari must be performed on the awakening-day in Kārtika, / from which countless merit is attained, O best of sages.
With fruits and various substances during the vigil on Prabodhinī, / taking water in a conch shell, an offering of water should be given to Janārdana.
Whatever fruit is attained at all holy places, whatever fruit in all charities, / that fruit is multiplied ten million times by offering water on the day of awakening.
Then worship of the guru should be performed with food, garments, and the like, / and with priestly gifts, O divine sage, for the satisfaction of the discus-bearing Lord.
The man who listens to the Bhāgavata or recites the Purāṇa / gains for every syllable the fruit born of the gift of a brown cow.
In Kārtika, O tiger among sages, he who performs the vow of Viṣṇu according to his capacity / and as prescribed, his liberation is firmly assured.
The one whose banner bears Garuḍa, Madhusūdana, when worshipped with a single leaf of ketakī, / remains well pleased for a thousand years.
One should worship the divine Janārdana with agasti flowers; / from his sight, O divine sage, the fire of hell is extinguished.
Viṣṇu, Puruṣottama, worshipped with munipuṣpa flowers in Kārtika, / grants desired wishes, as on an eclipse of the moon or sun.
Leaving aside all flowers, he who worships Keśava with the munipuṣpa flower / in Kārtika with devotion obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Those who offer tulasī leaves and flowers to Janārdana / in Kārtika, dear one, burn away all the sins of ten thousand births.
Seen, touched, or meditated upon, sung, praised by name, / planted, watered daily, and worshipped, the auspicious tulasī,
when people practice ninefold devotion to tulasī day by day, / they extend their virtuous deeds for thousands of tens of millions of yugas, O sage.
As long as the tulasī planted by men flourishes upon the earth / with branches, twigs, seeds, flowers, and leaves, O sage,
for that long, those born in their lineage—those who will be and those who have passed— / dwell in Hari's abode for a thousand kalpa years.
Whatever fruit lies in all flowers and in all leaves, O Nārada, / that is obtained in Kārtika by means of a single tulasī leaf.
Seeing that Kārtika has arrived, Janārdana, Mahāviṣṇu, / should be worshipped according to rule with tender tulasī leaves.
Having worshipped the gods with hundreds of sacrifices, having given gifts manifoldly, / that same merit is attained with tulasī leaves in the worship of Keśava in Kārtika.

6.62.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Lord, I wish to hear of the best vow among vows, / which takes away all sins, belongs to Viṣṇu, and grants the fruit to those who observe vows.
Tell me the story of the month of Puruṣottama, O Janārdana! / What is the procedure, what is its fruit, and which deity is worshipped there?
When an intercalary month has arrived, tell me the vow, O Janārdana! / What is the merit of which gift? What should be done by men, O Lord?
How should bathing be done, and what is the muttering [of mantras]? How is the procedure of worship taught? / What excellent food should be eaten in this month of Puruṣottama?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: / I shall relate to you, O king of kings, on account of my affection for you, / the glorification of the month of Puruṣottama, which destroys sins.
When an intercalary month has arrived, the eleventh lunar day that occurs / is known by the name Kamalā, the best lunar day among lunar days.
By the power of its vow, Kamalā becomes favorable. / Rising in the Brāhma-muhūrta and remembering Puruṣottama,
and having bathed according to rule, the vow-keeper should make the observance. / In a house, muttering [prayers] has single merit, but at a river it is traditionally said to be doubled;
in a cowshed it is above a thousandfold; in a fire-chamber it is a hundredfold; / in places sacred to Śiva, at sacred bathing places, and in the presence of deities;
a hundred thousandfold in the presence of Tulasī, and indeed endless in the presence of Viṣṇu. / In Avantī there was a certain best of the twice-born named Śivaśarman.
He had five sons, and the youngest was full of faults. / Then he was abandoned by his father, and forsaken by his own kinsmen and relatives.

Through the influence of his bad deeds, he went into a far-off forest. / Once, by the course of destiny, he arrived at the king of sacred places [Prayāga].

Emaciated by hunger, with a pitiful face, he bathed at the confluence of the three rivers, / searching there among the hermitages of the sages, afflicted with hunger.
he saw the excellent hermitage of the sage Harimitra there, / in the month of Puruṣottama, amid an assembly of people.
There in the hermitage, from the mouth of the brāhmaṇas who were narrating the sin-destroying story, / Kamalā was heard by him with faith:
the most meritorious eleventh lunar day, the grantor of enjoyment and liberation. / Jayaśarman, having heard according to rule this Kamalā lunar day,
the most meritorious eleventh lunar day, the grantor of enjoyment and liberation, / observed the vow along with them, staying then in an empty dwelling.
When midnight had fully arrived, Lakṣmī came there: / 'I grant a boon, O brāhmaṇa, through the power of Kamalā.'

Jayaśarman said: / 'Who are you? Whose are you, O woman with thighs like plantain trunks? And why are you pleased with me? / Are you Indrāṇī, [consort] of the lord of the gods, or Bhavānī, [consort] of Śaṅkara,
or a Gandharva woman, or a Kinnara woman, or the bride of the Moon or Sun? / One like you has never been seen nor heard of, O fair-faced woman!'
Lakṣmī said: / 'I have now become pleased; I have come from Vaikuṇṭha, / sent by the god of gods through the power of Kamalā.
The vow of that [eleventh day] which occurs in the first fortnight of the month of Puruṣottama / was performed by you at Prayāga in the presence of the sage.
Through the power of this vow, I am subservient [to you], there is no doubt. / Men will be born in your lineage, O best of the twice-born,
who through my grace will obtain [wealth]; the truth has been spoken to you by me.' / The brāhmaṇa said: 'If you are pleased, O Padmā, tell me the vow in detail,
whose stories the virtuous men and twice-born engage in.' / Lakṣmī said: 'It is the supreme thing to be heard by listeners, unexcelled among purifiers,
destroying bad dreams, meritorious; therefore it should be listened to with effort. / An excellent person endowed with faith, having recited a verse or even half a verse,
is immediately freed from tens of millions of heinous sins. / It is the supreme month among months, just as Garuḍa is among birds,
and as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and the twelfth lunar day is among lunar days. / Even today all the gods desire birth in Bhārata;
they worship that disease-free Nārāyaṇa in various ways. / Those who always worship the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa, with devotion,
are constantly worshipped by the hosts of deities headed by Brahmā. / Those who are devoted to the Name and intent on chanting the praises of Hari,
and those who are devoted to worshipping Hari have achieved their purpose in the Kali yuga. / Whether in the bright fortnight or in the dark fortnight, there may be two eleventh lunar days:

for householders the first is prescribed, and the latter is taught for ascetics. / When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days [combine], and the thirteenth is at the end of night, / there the merit of a hundred sacrifices is obtained at the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day.
'Having remained without food on the eleventh lunar day, I shall eat on the next day, / O lotus-eyed one! O Acyuta, be my refuge!'
Having uttered this mantra to the disc-bearer, the god of gods, / with a mind contented through devotional disposition, one should observe the fast.
Restrained, the vow-keeper should keep a vigil in front of the god / with songs, musical instruments, dances, and the recitation of Purāṇas and the like.
Then, having risen in the morning on the twelfth day, the vow-keeper, / having bathed, having worshipped Viṣṇu according to rule, with senses restrained,
having bathed Janārdana with the five nectars on the eleventh day, / and from a bath with milk on the twelfth day, enjoys the state of having the same form as Hari.
'For me, blinded by the darkness of ignorance, O Keśava, through this vow / be pleased, turn your face towards me, and be the grantor of the eye of knowledge.'
Having thus petitioned the lord of the gods, the god of gods, the mace-bearer, / he should feed brāhmaṇas with devotion and give them priestly gifts.
Then, together with his kinsmen, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, / having performed the five great sacrifices, he himself should eat with speech restrained.
Whoever, restrained, thus performs the meritorious vow of the eleventh lunar day / goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which return is hard to obtain.
Having spoken thus and granted him a boon, Kamalā disappeared; / he too, the Brahmin, became wealthy and went to his father's house.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: / Whoever thus performs the excellent vow of Kamalā, O king, / or hears it on the day of Viṣṇu, is freed from all sins.

6.63.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Many dharmas and vows have been heard, O Lord of the universe; / but nothing equal to the eleventh lunar day has been heard, O Janārdana!
Tell me again of an eleventh lunar day that destroys sin and bestows merit, / by performing which a man in this world may attain the supreme abode.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: / Whenever an eleventh lunar day occurs, whether in the bright or in the dark fortnight, / it should not be neglected, O protector of the earth, as it increases the happiness of liberation.
The eleventh lunar day in the Kali yuga, O king, releases one from the bondage of worldly existence; / it grants all desires and destroys sins among sins on earth.
On Sunday, or on an auspicious planetary transit, O best of kings, / the eleventh lunar day must always be fasted on; it increases sons and grandsons.
The vow of the eleventh lunar day must never be abandoned by those dear to Viṣṇu; / it constantly grants long life and fame, and bestows offspring, health, and wealth.
It grants liberation, beauty, and sovereignty—the eternal vow of the eleventh lunar day. / Those who perform it, O ruler of the earth, endowed with supreme faith,
according to the prescribed rule in the world—those men have the form of Viṣṇu. / Indeed, they are seen to be liberated while living, O king; there is no doubt about this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / How are they liberated while living, O Kṛṣṇa, and how are they forms of Viṣṇu, / yet they are seen to have the appearance of sinners? Indeed, I have great curiosity.
The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / Those who in the Kali age, O king, perform with devotion the supreme waterless vow / of Ekādaśī according to the prescribed rite,
how are they not forms of Viṣṇu? How are they not liberated while living? / There is no merit equal to the Ekādaśī vow, which removes all sin,
and nothing is known, O king, that grants all desires to human beings. / Eating once on Daśamī, and observing a waterless vow on Nandā,
and breaking the fast on Bhadrā, men become equal to Viṣṇu. / A faithful person who undertakes the auspicious Kāmadā vow
attains their desired wish both in this world and the next. / For this [vow] is pure, purifying, and destroys the greatest sins,
and it bestows enjoyment and liberation upon its observers, O best of kings. / On Kāmadā, one should worship Puruṣottama according to the rules,
with flowers, incense, and the like, and with various offerings of food. / Bell-metal, meat, lentils, chickpeas, and kodrava grains,
greens, honey, food belonging to another, eating a second time, and sexual intercourse: / a Vaiṣṇava undertaking the vow should avoid these ten on Daśamī.
Gambling, playing, sleeping, betel, brushing the teeth, / speaking ill of others, backbiting, stealing, violence, and sexual pleasure,
anger, and false speech: one must avoid these on Ekādaśī. / Bell-metal, meat, lentils, oil, untruthful speech,
exercise, travel, eating a second time, sexual intercourse, / riding on a bull, food belonging to another, and greens on the Dvādaśī day.
Those by whom the Kāmadā [vow] has been performed according to this rule, O king, / keeping a vigil at night and worshipping Puruṣottama,
freed from all sins, go to the supreme state. / From reciting or hearing it, O king, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

6.64.m: Nārada said: / Whatever observances during Cāturmāsya are renowned on earth, / I wish to hear them; speak of them, O Maheśvara.
What is to be done during Cāturmāsya when Hari, Janārdana, is asleep? / Tell me, O Lord, what fruit is gained by giving up the six tastes, by keeping nails and hair, / and by other observances.
Sūta said: / Having heard this, the god smiled with blooming eyes, / and spoke to that best of twice-borns, Nārada, a storehouse of asceticism.
Mahādeva said: / Listen here, O divine sage, I will explain it in detail. / Fasting on the Ekādaśī of the bright half of Āṣāḍha,
one should undertake here the Cāturmāsya vows with devotion. / Taking to a bed upon the ground when Hari has entered yogic sleep,
one should spend the four months until the full moon of Kārttika arrives. / Consecrations do not take place, nor rituals such as sacrifices,
marriages, investiture with vows, and other auspicious rites, / royal journeys, expeditions, and other diverse activities.
When the Lord of the World, Acyuta, whose banner bears Garuḍa, is asleep, / hear the fruit of the vow for whoever performs the rite of the vow.
Whatever fruit a man obtains through a thousand horse sacrifices, / he obtains that very fruit through the observed Cāturmāsya vows.
When the thousand-rayed sun is in Gemini, one should put Madhusūdana to sleep; / when the sun has moved into the constellation of Libra, one should awaken Hari again.
Even if an intercalary month occurs, this is the sequence of the rule: / one should set up an image of Viṣṇu bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
dressed in yellow garments, gentle, and placed on a pure couch / covered with a white cloth and provided with a pillow, O Nārada,
One who knows legendary history and the Purāṇas, or else a devotee of Viṣṇu, / having bathed [the deity] with curd, milk, honey, parched grains, and ghee,
and smeared it with auspicious perfumes, with incense and delightful flowers, / worshipped with white blossoms, [he should recite] with this mantra, O brāhmaṇa:
“When you are asleep, O Lord of the World, this universe falls asleep; / when you are awake, all this universe, moving and unmoving, awakens.”
Having thus established that image of Viṣṇu, O Nārada, / one should then personally undertake the observance in its presence with spoken words.
A woman or a man devoted to him, according to the distinction of dharma and adharma, / for the four rainy months, up to the awakening of the god,
should undertake these observances, preceded by cleaning the teeth. / Then, having fasted, when the dawn is clear,
having performed the daily rite in the presence of Viṣṇu, with self-control, / I shall proclaim the separate fruits of those who perform them.
A wise man obtains sweetness by avoiding molasses; / likewise, a long lineage is obtained from avoiding oil.
From avoiding ghee, O brāhmaṇa, he is born with a handsome body; / one who renounces mustard oil attains the destruction of enemies.
By giving up scented oil, he obtains incomparable good fortune; / one who renounces the enjoyment of flowers becomes a Vidyādhara in heaven.
A man who practices yoga attains the abode of Brahmā. / The six tastes—pungent, sour, sweet, salty, bitter, and astringent—
whoever avoids them, that man never incurs deformity or foul odor. / By avoiding betel, a man of enjoyment is born with a melodious throat.
From giving up ghee comes loveliness, and his body is always radiant; / and from giving up fruit, O best of brāhmaṇas, he is born with many sons.
One who eats from palāśa leaves becomes handsome and endowed with enjoyments; / radiant and causing light, he becomes a lord of wealth in person.
One who renounces curd and milk, that man attains Goloka; / whoever observes a vow of silence, his command becomes unfailing.
He attains the throne of Indra by avoiding cooked grain offerings. / By renouncing these and other such things, he abides in dharma, a son of dharma.
Having recited “Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa,” he gains a hundredfold fruit; / he alone indeed becomes the lord of Vidyādharas in heaven.
By a mere bath at Puṣkara, the fruit produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā [is obtained].
He who always eats upon the ground becomes a ruler of the earth; / and one who performs smearing and sweeping in a temple of Viṣṇu
remains for a kalpa in Vaikuṇṭha, O wise one; there is no doubt about this. / And the man who performs circumambulation a hundred and eight times
departs together with a divine celestial chariot drawn by swans. / One who performs vocal and instrumental music for Viṣṇu attains the world of the Gandharvas.
Eating the five products of the cow, O wise one, he gains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; / and whoever constantly enlightens people through the pleasure of the scriptures,
assuming the form of Vyāsa before Viṣṇu, attains from there the abode of Viṣṇu. / Having performed worship with tulasī leaves, one goes to Viṣṇu's realm.
Having performed divine sprinkling, he obtains the abode of the Apsarases; / by bathing at home with cold water, he attains a stainless body.
By renouncing hot water, one truly gains the bath of Puṣkara; / the man who eats from leaves gains the fruit of Kurukṣetra.
Whoever constantly eats upon a stone, his is the merit born of Prayāga; / a man who renounces water at dawn is not overcome by illnesses.
Eating from copper vessels, one attains the fruit of Naimiṣa. / Having abandoned a bronze vessel, one should use the remaining vessels.
If no vessels at all are available, an earthen vessel is the best; / or else with vessels made from palāśa [leaves], gathered by oneself.
If a wise person maintains the agnihotra for a full year, / or takes meals from [palāśa] leaf-vessels, that is considered equal to it.
Eating from brahma-leaves is declared to be equal to the cāndrāyaṇa penance; / each single meal, O wise one, taken by one eating from brahma-leaves,
is declared equal to a three-night fast, destroying the great sins. / Whatever merit is proclaimed from fasting on an Ekādaśī,
and the fruit of all gifts, and the fruit of all sacred fords one obtains; / nor does one see hell, from eating off lotus leaves.
A brāhmaṇa goes to Vaikuṇṭha, while another person attains heaven. / This is the great tree of Brahmā, which removes sin and grants all desires.
The middle leaf is forbidden to the śūdra caste, O best of kings; / eating from it, he incurs hell for as long as fourteen Indras [rule].
He should avoid the middle leaf; eating is [permitted] on the other leaves. / If a śūdra eats from the middle leaf, O twice-born,
purification occurs by giving a brown cow to a brāhmaṇa, and not otherwise. / If a śūdra milks a brown cow and consumes [the milk] in his own house,
he is born as a worm in excrement for ten thousand years. / Released from the womb of a worm, he enters the womb of a beast.
If one who has become a śūdra hitches a brown ox here, / for as many hairs as it has, for that many years, O Nārada,
that man will be cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells; of this there is no doubt. / Especially if there is a she-goat in that śūdra's house,
by drinking her milk, a śūdra indeed goes to Raurava. / A śūdra who is seen to engage in trade along with brāhmaṇas—
that vipra becomes excluded from the Veda, and the śūdra is called a Kaulika. / A vipra who is urged into trade and carries out a śūdra's command,
becomes a dweller of hell for as many steps as he walks. / A vipra who is sent into a house by a śūdra for the purpose of water—
having drunk that water, which is like intoxicating liquor, he surely goes to hell. / A gift should always and constantly be given to a twice-born by a śūdra,
and devotion toward them especially ought to be practiced. / Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes to the next world.
Indeed, this [body] composed of the five elements is declared useless; / therefore, it should indeed be given to the guru, from which one obtains endless fruit.
In this terrible Kali yuga of sinful conduct, wicked people / revile people of meritorious deeds, O chief of vipras.
Through reviling, one obtains misery until the dissolution of all beings. / Various dharmas are set in motion in the Kali age, O wise one.
This dharma is rare in the world, bestowing dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation. / Whatever man lies upon the ground on the earth's surface,
is not afflicted by diseases for ten thousand years; / that man is born having many sons, endowed with riches, and free from leprosy.
A man who eats only at night obtains the fruit of pilgrimage to sacred fords; / and by eating food unasked for, he attains the fruit of constructing reservoirs and wells.
One who avoids hostility and turns away from harming living beings [is praised], / for "Non-violence is the supreme dharma," as is sung in the Vedas.
"Giving, compassion, and self-restraint," has been heard by me everywhere. / Therefore, it must be practiced with all effort, even by great souls.
Those who surrender their body, sons, and grandsons to the guru / attain the state of being dear to Viṣṇu through the power of that gift.
One initiated by a śūdra, and a śūdra initiated by a śūdra— / both of them are declared sinners until the dissolution of all beings.
When a śūdra, foremost among sinners, sets his mind on violence, / twenty-one generations of his family are cast down to hell by him.
In the Kali age, many heretical śūdras are seen on earth; / merely from conversing with them, hell ensues, O twice-born.
Those who are devoted to the knowledge of Brahman and chant the Gāyatrī, O twice-born— / merely by the sight of those [heretics], there is the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa day after day.
Vipras who bear the conch and discus, who are committed to the duties of Viṣṇu, / constantly devoted to Vedic dharma, purify even those who purify the assembly.
This observance of Cāturmāsya must always be performed by those men. / What else is there to say at length again and again, O brāhmaṇa?
Blessed are those men on earth who are Vaiṣṇavas in this world; / their lineage is considered most blessed, and their birth most blessed.
He who eats honey while the divine Janārdana is asleep / incurs great sin. Hear what results from avoiding it:
Whatever fruit is attained through all various sacrifices, one obtains that. / One should avoid pomegranate, citron, and coconut.
Becoming a god riding an aerial chariot, he goes at the end to Viṣṇu's abode; / he is born wealthy, fortunate, and in a prosperous family.
A man who spends the four months eating only once a day— / for as many moments as the sun has risen and risen,
for so many thousands of years he is exalted in the world of Viṣṇu. / And the human being who avoids rice, barley, and wheat,
obtains whatever fruit has been declared by the sages / when a horse sacrifice or other rite is performed according to rule with sacrificial gifts.
He is born endowed with wealth and grain, and possessing many sons. / Those who perform ancestral libations with tulasī, sesame seeds, and darbha grass,
that fruit of theirs is multiplied ten-millionfold, especially during Cāturmāsya. / When Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, if one should perform it endowed with these three,
they also rejoice in the presence of Viṣṇu for thousands of yugas. / Those who sing a quarter-verse or half a quarter-verse, or a verse or half-verse
in front of Viṣṇu, are liberated; of this there is no doubt. / He who avoids sexual intercourse while the divine Janārdana is asleep,
is also exalted in the world of Viṣṇu for one manvantara. / Curd, milk, as well as buttermilk, jaggery, and likewise vegetables—
merely by abstaining from these, O vipra, one partakes in liberation; of this there is no doubt. / Those human beings who take their bath with myrobalan,
day after day they obtain great merit, O sage. / The wise declare the dhātrī fruit to be a destroyer of sins.
Formerly, brāhmaṇas were created for the deliverance of the three worlds. / He who observes silence at twilight and eats [thus] for the four months,
rejoices again in Vaikuṇṭha for four manvantaras. / A man who cooks his own food and eats [thus] for the four months,
is exalted in the world of Indra for ten thousand years. / And one should observe silence during the four months of the rainy season;
he will go to the city of Viṣṇu, and immediately thereafter to Brahman, O brāhmaṇa. / A man who eats in silence never suffers distress.
Even rākṣasas went to heaven by eating in silence. / Cooked food that is mixed with worms and insects becomes impure;
such food should also be known as equal to cow's meat, O best of the twice-born. / If a human being swallows that food, it is to be known as impure.
This meal is declared to be always pleasing to the rākṣasas; / for Brahmā was gratified formerly, and it was granted by that great soul.
Having fed [others] in silence, he has attained heaven; of this there is no doubt. / But he who eats while chattering—by that his food becomes impure.
He eats pure sin; therefore, one should observe silence. / Food taken in silence should be known to be equal to fasting, O Nārada.
The best of men who eats in silence during the five prāṇa-oblations, / his five great sins are destroyed without any doubt.
One should not wear patched cloth during rites for the ancestors, O brāhmaṇa; / and cloth kept on an impure part of the body becomes impure.
If someone passes stool while the cloth is on the hips and back, / or urinates, or engages in sexual intercourse, he should discard that cloth.
It must especially be avoided in rites for the ancestors, O brāhmaṇa. / And always, O sage, worship of the deity holding the discus
must be performed especially by the pure, with subdued senses. / While Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, grass, vegetables, safflower,
and stitched garments should be avoided with effort. / During the four months, while Hari is asleep, whoever avoids these
does not go to hell until the dissolution of all beings. / One should not consume alcohol or meat, nor hare or pork.
Especially during the four months, while god Janārdana is asleep, / a man devoted to non-violence attains divinity.
Falsehood, anger, harshness, and sexual intercourse on festival days— / whoever avoids these, O best of brāhmaṇas, gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
In celibacy lies increase of offspring, as well as increase of lifespan. / Flowers, leaves, fruit, a bed, oil massage, and ointment,
milk not used in sacrifice, meat, and liquor—one should avoid these. / During the four months, while Hari is asleep, whatever has been given up by vow
must first be given to a brāhmaṇa, without a doubt. / That wealth given to a twice-born becomes imperishable, O wise one;
he receives it multiplied millions of times, O brāhmaṇa, there is no doubt of this. / By whatever observance Hari is worshipped, O best of brāhmaṇas,
he grants the abode of Viṣṇu—no hesitation should be made here. / Whoever does not undertake an observance during the four months while Hari is asleep,
he goes to hell, and his life has passed in vain. / Whatever excellent rule stated by the twice-born a man constantly observes,
and the observances so stated, he goes to the highest abode. / A gift given devoid of the three aims of life becomes fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, the best of men should please Janārdana, / the god of gods, through observances and gifts according to his capacity.
Without bathing, giving gifts, and worship of brāhmaṇas, / all that has gone in vain as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Nārada said: / Tell me, O Lord, ruler of the universe, what kind of celibacy is it / by the practice of which Govinda becomes fully satisfied with men?
Mahādeva said: / One who is devoted only to his own wife is considered celibate by the wise. / A man who abandons his own wife is lower than a Cāṇḍāla, O learned one.
Approaching her only in her fertile season is prescribed as celibacy. / Whoever abandons a devoted wife who is free from fault,
that evil-doing man incurs [the guilt of] killing an embryo in this world. / Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices
are not worth a sixteenth part of a fast on the eleventh lunar day. / Bathing, giving gifts, silent recitation, fire-offering, recitation of sacred texts, and worship of the deity—
whatever is performed during the four months becomes imperishable. / Whoever listens to a Purāṇa once or twice a day,
freed from all sins, goes to the world of Viṣṇu. / Especially while Hari is asleep, by reciting and chanting the name of Hari,
one obtains that fruit multiplied ten million times, O best of the twice-born. / A brāhmaṇa who is a Vaiṣṇava, who performs worship,

is indeed entirely righteous and truly worthy of honor, without a doubt. / This merit of the four months is pure and destroys sins; / by hearing it, one gains merit and obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.

6.65.m: Nārada said: / Speak of the concluding rite for the vows of the four months, O Lord. / When the concluding rite is performed, everything certainly becomes complete.
Mahādeva said: / Having undertaken a vow, O fortunate one, if one does not perform the concluding rite, / that performer of rites does not fully partake of the fruit.
By falling into a defect in the vow, one is born a leper and blind. / For this reason, O twice-born, one must perform the concluding rite.
Having undertaken these observances and maintained them according to the rules, / when the Lord of the World has awakened from sleep, one should go into the presence of a brāhmaṇa,
and beg forgiveness from the god of gods according to rule and in detail. / For giving up oil, one should give clarified butter; for giving up clarified butter, milk is prescribed.
For [a vow of] silence, balls of food with sesame seeds and gold should be given to a twice-born. / For [a vow concerning] eating, one should give food accompanied by curd-rice.
One should especially give food accompanied by gold. / By the gift of food, O best of sages, one is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
A man who eats from a leaf-plate of palāśa for four months / should give a vessel full of clarified butter at the concluding rite, O twice-born.
One should give a meal of six flavors to a brāhmaṇa for [the vow of] eating at night. / For the vow of unasked food, he should give a bull along with gold.
For abstaining from black gram, O best of sages, he should give a cow along with her calf. / For bathing with myrobalan, a man should give a māṣa-weight of gold.
For an observance concerning fruits, he should give fruits; / for an observance concerning grains, grain or rice is prescribed.
Likewise, for sleeping on the ground, a bed with a cotton mattress and a pillow [should be given]. / If celibacy was maintained during the four months, O best of the twice-born,
a meal should be given to a married couple, to both of them with devotion, / accompanied by enjoyment, together with a priestly fee, and with vegetables and salt.
For daily bathing, a man should give ghee and roasted barley flour for [abstaining from] unguents. / In a vow concerning nails and hair, he should present a span-length [mirror].
Two shoes should be given for abstaining from shoes. / For giving up meat, a tawny cow with her calf is prescribed.
He who continually offers lamps should bring a golden lamp; / he should give that lamp, filled with clarified butter, to a twice-born,
to a brāhmaṇa devoted to Viṣṇu, desiring completion of the vow. / For the observance of vegetables, vegetables [should be given]; for black gram, a golden māṣa.
For the observance of abstaining from intercourse, one should give silver to a twice-born. / For the observance concerning betel-leaf, camphor along with gold [should be given].
From time to time, O best of the twice-born, whatever was practiced as a vow, / that very item should especially be given, desiring to attain the other world.

Having first performed bathing and the like, one should reveal it before Viṣṇu. / The god without beginning or end bears the conch, discus, and mace; / before him, why would they not do so, since Viṣṇu is the remover of sins?

6.66.m: Nārada said: / Speak of the propitiation of Yama for my welfare, O best of gods, / [and] how a man does not go into the midst of hell, O Lord.
It is heard that in the world of Yama there is ever the Vaitaraṇī river, / invincible, boundless, impassable, and full of blood.
Impasseable for all beings, how can it become easily crossed? / There is this fear regarding the world of Yama, O Lord Mahādeva.
For liberation from that, tell me all that must be done, / O blessed one, ruler of the gods, having taken pity on me.
Mahādeva said: / Formerly in Dvāravatī, O brāhmaṇa, having bathed in the salt ocean, / I saw a sage coming, a brāhmaṇa named Mudgala,
blazing like the sun, his limbs shining with ascetic heat. / Bowing to me, the sage Mudgala, filled with wonder, spoke:
Mudgala said: / Suddenly fainting, O god, I fell upon the surface of the earth; / my limbs burned, seized by the servants of Yama.
Dragged by force, a person only the size of a thumb, / bound fast by Yama's soldiers, I was taken into the presence of Śamana.
In an instant I saw in the assembly hall Yama with reddish-brown eyes, / a dark face, exceedingly fierce, surrounded by hundreds of diseases and forms of death,
attended by the personified disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm, / by emaciation of the body, fevers, terror, boils, spiders, and the like,
by burning sensations, body-aches, headaches, fistula, and loss of strength, / by scrofula, eye-diseases, dysuria, fevers, and sores,
by fainting fits, choking, heart-diseases, evil spirits, and thieves— / thus by many kinds of fierce, diverse, terrifying forms;
by those holding skulls and severed heads in their hands, on the battlefield and in hell, / by fierce rākṣasas and dānavas seated and standing before him,
by officers of justice and scribes headed by Citragupta, / by tigers, lions, boars, and very uncontrollable crested serpents,
by scorpions, fanged creatures, spirits, worms, bedbugs, and the like, / by wolves, variegated dogs, herons, vultures, and jackals,
by thieves, spirits of poverty, plagues, and seizing ḍākinīs, / with disheveled hair, sighs and coughs, their faces contorted with frowns,
of great prowess, unfearing, punishers of evil deeds. / Yama shone in the assembly, attended by his retinue
and by terrifying forest creatures, like an antimony mountain with serpents. / Then the lord of the universe spoke with restraint to his servants:
“How was a sage brought by you, confused by the name? / The son of Bhīmaka in the village of Kauṇḍinya is named Mudgala;
he is a kṣatriya whose lifespan has ended, he is to be brought—let this one be released!” / Hearing this, they departed from him and immediately returned.
All those servants of Yama said again to Dharmarāja: / “When we went there, no embodied being whose lifespan has ended was perceived.”
Yama said: / “What is the reason that men are generally invisible to you? / [They are invisible] through the well-performed Dvādaśī, celebrated as the Vaitaraṇī river,
or those who have died in Ujjayinī, at Prayāga, or at the Yamunā, / or those by whom sesame seeds, elephants, gold, and the like, and daily food for cows has been given.”
The messengers said: / “What kind of vow is that, O brāhmaṇa? Tell everything without remainder! / What is to be done there by men, O god, that gives you satisfaction?
By whom has the Dvādaśī born of the dark fortnight been observed, O best of men, / and by what fasting is one freed from sin?
By what rite is that vow to be performed? Speak truly! / Being well pleased, you must speak, taking pity, O treasure of mercy!”
The illustrious Mudgala said: / Hearing the words of the messengers, he then spoke sweetly: / “I shall tell everything, O messengers, just as seen, just as heard.”
Yama said: / “In the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, those which belong to the dark fortnight— / on their previous [tithis], O messengers, according to the rule, is the Vaitaraṇī vow.
It should be performed every month until a year is certainly reached. / Having performed it, O messengers, one is freed—of this there is no doubt.
The observance of fasting, which grants pleasure to Viṣṇu, is to be performed: / ‘Today, O Lord of the gods of gods, my fast will take place;
on the Dvādaśī, Govinda is to be worshipped, endowed with a devotional disposition. / Whatever eating or sexual intercourse [has occurred] in sleep through infirmity of the senses,
forgive all that, O god, showing mercy upon me.’ / Having made such an observance, one should go at midday to a sacred bathing place.
Taking clay, cow dung, and sesame seeds, one should go according to the rule. / A bath is to be performed there for the completion of the vow.
With the mantra beginning ‘Aśvakrānte’, one should especially take a bath: / ‘O you stepped upon by horses, stepped upon by chariots, stepped upon by Viṣṇu, O earth,
O clay, take away my sin that was accumulated by me previously!’ / By the sin destroyed by it, one is freed from all sins.
Sesame seeds produced in Kāśī indeed have the form of Viṣṇu. / By a bath with sesame seeds, Govinda removes all sin.
‘O goddess born from the body of Viṣṇu, taking away great sins, / take away all the sin of all [people] indeed; homage be to you!’
Holding a tulasī leaf and reciting the names [of the Lord] beforehand, / a bath is declared by the virtuous to be performed according to the rule.
Having bathed thus, stepped out, and put on two clean garments, / having gratified the ancestors and the gods, then indeed comes the worship of Viṣṇu.
Having set up an unblemished jar joined with five sprouts, / endowed with the five jewels, perfumed with divine garlands and fragrance,
filled with water, accompanied by precious things and a copper vessel, / [worship] the god Śrīdhara situated there, the god of gods, the treasure of austerities.
With the complete rite, O king, one should perform the most exalted worship. / One should cause to be made an auspicious mandala prepared with clay, cow dung, and the like,
and one should make it with clean washed rice ground with a stone. / Dharmarāja is to be fashioned, endowed with hands and other limbs.
Having placed a copper Vaitaraṇī river in front of him, / one should worship it separately and properly, with an invocation beforehand:
‘I invoke the lord of the gods, Yama, whose form is the universe; / come here, O greatly fortunate one, make your presence felt, O Keśava!
This is water for the feet, O beloved of Śrī, seated, O Lord Hari! / You who always delight in the cosmic garden, show mercy upon me.’
‘Homage to the giver of prosperity’—the feet; ‘and to the sorrowless one’—the knees; / ‘homage to Śiva’—the thighs; ‘to the one whose form is the universe’—the waist;
‘homage to Kandarpa’—the penis; ‘and to the Āditya’—the scrotum; / ‘to Dāmodara’—the belly; ‘and to Vāsudeva’—the breasts;
‘to Śrīdhara’—the face; ‘to Keśava’—the hair; / ‘to the wielder of the bow Śārṅga’—the back; ‘and to the granter of boons’—the feet;

by his own name: ‘to the one who holds the conch, discus, sword, mace, and axe in hand, / homage to you, the Self of all’—the head is thus addressed.

To the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, and the Dwarf, / to Rāma, to Rāma, and to Kṛṣṇa, to the Wise One, and to Kalki, homage be to you!
‘For the sake of destroying the flood of all sins, I worship; homage, homage!’ / And having meditated upon Viṣṇu with all these mantras, one should worship him.
‘O Dharmarāja, homage be to you; O Dharmarāja, homage be to you! / Homage to you, the lord of the southern direction, whose mount is a buffalo!
Homage to you, O Citragupta; homage, homage to Vicitra! / For the sake of pacifying the torments of hell, grant my desired wishes.’
To Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Death, and to the Ender, / to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings,
to Vṛkodara, to Citra, and homage to Citragupta, / to Nīla, and to Dadhan, one should always offer homage, homage.
Thus the lord Dharmarāj is to be worshipped with the twelve names. / ‘O Vaitaraṇī, very difficult to cross, destroyer of sin, grantor of all desires,
come here, O greatly fortunate one; accept the offering of water made by me! / The Vaitaraṇī river is renowned along the terrible path to the gate of Yama.’
for delivering [souls] from her, which transcends birth, death, and old age, / which is impassable for evildoers and takes away the fear of all living beings,
in which living beings, intent on torment, sink out of fear— / desiring to cross that dreadful [river], O Goddess Jayā, homage, homage to you!
The gods dwell in her, that Vaitaraṇī river; / and she too is worshipped with devotion for the pleasure of Keśava,
upon whose bank the sages enter, as do the ancestors; / and she too, worshipped in the form of a river, removes sins.
I will give her so that [you] may cross, for liberation from all sins; / for the sake of religious merit, I shall declare to you the Vaitaraṇī river:
“You have been worshipped by me with devotion and for the pleasure of Keśava. / O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Universe, deliver me from cyclic existence!
Take away all my sin by the mere utterance of your name! / This supreme sacred thread is made of nine threads;
accept it, O Lord of Gods, and, being pleased, grant me what is desired! / This betel-leaf is offered to you, most splendid according to my ability;
accept it, O Lord of Gods, and deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence! / This five-wick lamp is your waving of lights, O Lord of Gods,
O sun to the darkness of delusion, endowed with devotion, removing the affliction of worldly existence! / Excellent food, well-cooked rice-dish, endowed with all flavors,
has been offered by me with devotion, O Blessed One; let it be accepted!” / And with the twelve-syllable mantra, recited according to number:
“May the beloved of Śrī be pleased with me, and, being pleased, grant what is wished!” / Five cows were produced when the great ocean was churned;
among them, to the cow that is Nandā, homage, homage to that wish-fulfilling cow! / Having worshipped the cow according to rule, collected in mind, one should present the water-offering:
“O Goddess yielding all desires, warding off universal destruction, / grant health, long-lasting progeny, and food, O Nandā, always to me!
Worshipped by Vasiṣṭha and by the wise Viśvāmitra, / O brown cow, take away my sin that was accumulated formerly by me!
May cows be in front of me, may cows be behind me; / may cows with golden horns, pouring out milk, attend upon me in heaven!
Surabhi and her daughters, just as rivers are to the ocean; / O Goddess containing all gods, O very auspicious one, loving to your devotees,
Having thus worshipped according to rule, one should give daily food to the cows: / “O daughters of Surabhi, beneficent to all, pure, destroyers of sins!”
may the cows, mothers of the three worlds, accept my mouthful!” / “Gaṃ, homage to the mace for the sake of prosperity and for the destruction of all sins.”
By this very mantra the wise one should bear the mace; / “Paṃ, homage to Padmanābha,” the intelligent one should bear the lotus;
“Caṃ, to Viṣṇu having the form of the discus,” the bearing born of the discus is taught; / “Śaṃ, homage be to you who have the form of the conch, bringer of happiness,”
by this mantra indeed, O messengers, the bearing born of the conch is taught. / The bearing of the four weapons is taught by the sages:
just as the agnihotra is daily, and study of the Veda likewise, / so too is this bearing of the heated seals and the rest for a brāhmaṇa,
with fragrant sandalwood, and indeed with gopīcandana clay— / especially the bearing by brāhmaṇas who have crossed to the far shore of the Veda.
Even an outcaste becomes pure from bearing it, without a doubt, / if he wears an upright, straight, gentle forehead mark with the insignia.
Even that outcaste, pure in soul, is always worthy of worship by the twice-born. / In the house of outcastes, O messengers, wherever a tulasī is seen,
the tulasī from that place should be taken with a devotional disposition of mind.

6.67.m: Maheśvara said: / Having heard this from the mouth of Dharma, Mudgala, the best of the twice-born, / having related it right before me, went away as he pleased, O sage.
Wherever gopīcandana stays, O best of the twice-born, / that house has the nature of a sacred site, as was indeed spoken by Viṣṇu.
Grief and delusion do not remain there; nowhere does misfortune occur / in the dwelling of that twice-born where gopīcandana is present.
Their ancestors are happy; their lineage increases always; / in whose house gopīcandana is present day and night.
The clay born of the cowherdesses’ Puṣkara is pure and cleanses the body; / through anointing with it, physical diseases and mental distress are destroyed.
Therefore, when borne on the body by men, it grants liberation and yields all desires. / Sacred sites roar only as long, and sacred fields always [roar] only as long,
as gopīcandana has not been seen nor heard, O twice-born. / This is to be meditated upon; this is to be worshipped, destroying impurities and faults;
by the mere touch of which a mortal becomes purified; / and at the time of death for mortals, it grants liberation and is supremely purifying.
What shall I say, O best of the twice-born? Gopīcandana grants liberation! / The tulasī wood of Viṣṇu, and also the soil from its roots,
and gopīcandana, and also haricandana— / having mixed these four, the wise one should rub his body.
By that, every sacred site on Jambūdvīpa is visited at all times. / But whoever makes a forehead mark with the paste of gopīcandana,
completely freed from all sin, goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. / By him the ancestral rites and other ceremonies of his father have been performed having gone to Gayā,
by whatever man gopīcandana has been worn. / A drinker of liquor, a killer of a brāhmaṇa, or a cow-killer, or a slayer of a child— / he is freed that very moment from wearing gopīcandana.

6.68.m: Maheśvara said: / Listen, O Nārada, I will tell the characteristic mark of Vaiṣṇavas,
having heard which, a person is freed from sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa. / What sort of characteristic mark they have, and what sort of nature they possess,
listen now, O tiger among sages, as I tell it just so: / Because he belongs to Viṣṇu, therefore he is called a Vaiṣṇava.
And among all the castes, a Vaiṣṇava is declared the best. / In the family of those whose food is most holy, a Vaiṣṇava [is born].
In whom forbearance, compassion, austerity, and truth abide, O twice-born, / by the mere sight of them sin is destroyed like cotton.
Whose mind is freed from the practice of injury and rests in Viṣṇu, / who always wears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
and who wears a garland made of tulasī wood around his neck, / [and] the wise one who always wears twelve kinds of forehead marks,
and who knows dharma and adharma—he is called a Vaiṣṇava; / he is always devoted to the Vedas and treatises, always a sacrificer of sacrifices,
and they perform twenty-four festivals again and again. / Their family is the most blessed; their fame is proclaimed;
they are indeed the most blessed people in the world, having become devotees of the Lord. / In whose family even one person is born as a devotee of the Lord,
by him that family is saved again and again, O brāhmaṇa. / Those born of eggs, those sprouting from shoots, and those born of a womb—
they all are to be recognized as bearers of the conch, discus, and mace, / by the mere sight of whom a killer of a brāhmaṇa is always purified.
However, I shall tell, O divine sage: more blessed than they on earth / are the Vaiṣṇavas who are seen in this world, O great sage.
They are indeed to be known as equal to Viṣṇu by those who know the truth; / they are heard by me to be the most fortunate in the world in the Kali age, without a doubt.
Viṣṇu was worshipped by him, the worship of all was performed, / [and] a great gift was given by him by whom Vaiṣṇavas have been worshipped.
Those who offer a fruit, a leaf, also vegetables, / or food, or indeed clothing to Vaiṣṇavas, are always fortunate on earth.
By whom a Vaiṣṇava is worshipped, worship of all is indeed performed; / they by whom Viṣṇu is worshipped are considered the most fortunate.
By the mere sight of them, a man is purified from sin. / What need is there to say more and more, O brāhmaṇa?
Therefore, the sight of them, and in touch, brings happiness. / As Viṣṇu is, so is he; there is never any difference anywhere.
Knowing this, O child, a wise man should worship at all times. / If even a single Vaiṣṇava Brahmin is fed on earth, / a thousand twice-born have been fed by him; of this there is no doubt.

6.69.m: Nārada said: / For those incapable of fasting, O best of gods, / always speak to me of that single meritorious Dvādaśī, O sinless one.
Śiva said: / In the month of Bhādrapada, in the bright fortnight, the Dvādaśī combined with Śravaṇa, / that indeed is all-bestowing, meritorious, and brings great fruit in fasting.
Having bathed at the confluence of rivers and fasted on that Dvādaśī, / one effortlessly attains the fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs.
And the Dvādaśī that is conjoined with Wednesday and Śravaṇa / is exceedingly great; everything done on it is imperishable.
When the Dvādaśī is joined with Śravaṇa, O Nārada, / having bathed at the confluence of rivers, one obtains the fruit born of the gift of a cow.
Having placed a jar filled with water, the wise man / should place a vessel upon it, having installed Janārdana.
Then in front of him, an offering of food cooked in ghee should be given; / and the wise man should give nine new jars containing water, according to his capacity.
Having worshipped Govinda thus, one should keep a vigil there. / At clear dawn, having bathed and worshipped the one whose banner is Garuḍa,
with flowers, incense, food offerings, and very beautiful fruits and garments, / one should then offer a handful of flowers and recite this mantra:
'Obeisance, obeisance to you, O Govinda, joined with Wednesday and Śravaṇa! / Having destroyed the mass of sins, become the bestower of all happiness.'
He should have pure food duly given to a brāhmaṇa / who has reached the end of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, especially to one who knows the Purāṇas.
By this rule, on the bank of a river, the best of men / should perform everything properly, even being intent with a single-pointed mind.
Here, too, they cite this ancient legendary history / of what occurred in a great forest. Hear it, O earthly god.
Hearing which, a human is freed from great distress in the world. / There was a region named Dāsaraka, and in the western part of it,
there, O wise one, is a desert region, terrifying to all creatures, / a land of intensely heated sand, where there are wicked great serpents,
thronged with trees of little shade, teeming with dead creatures, / along with *śamī*, *khadira*, *palāśa*, *karīra*, and *pīlu* trees.
There dreadful groups of trees are formed with strong thorns; / where the ground is seen in places crowded with eaten living creatures,
Yet all living beings live bound by their past actions; / there is no water, no reservoirs of water, nor any clouds there, O learned one.
Together with some thirsty young ones sheltered inside their wings, / the best of birds were seen, O brāhmaṇa, their lives departing.
In such a region, a certain merchant, under the sway of destiny, / separated from his caravan, entered the desert thicket.
With an agitated heart, afflicted with fatigue from hunger and thirst, he wandered. / 'Where is a village? Where is water? Where will I go?' He did not understand.
Then he saw spirits (*preta*s), their senses distressed by hunger and thirst, / monstrous, wicked, terrifying, fleshless, and fierce in appearance.
He saw one mounted on the shoulder of a spirit, deformed in appearance, / surrounded on all sides by many spirits,
approaching, exceedingly fierce, preceded by the sounds of spirits. / The spirit, too, having seen the man who had come to that dreadful forest,
going to the earth from the shoulder of the spirit, approached near him. / Having bowed down to the best of merchants, he spoke this word:
'How did your entrance occur into this most terrifying region?' / To him the wise merchant spoke: 'Of me, fallen away from a caravan in the forest,
the entrance was by the conjunction of destiny and done by past karma. / Thirst afflicts me exceedingly, and likewise hunger severely.
The end of my life has arrived; my speech seems to waver. / I do not see any means here by which I may somehow live.'
When this was said, the ghost addressed these words to that merchant: / “Take refuge under a blooming śamī tree and wait for a moment.”
Given hospitality by me, you will depart afterward as you please.' / Addressed thus, that merchant, tormented by thirst, did so.
When the time of midday arrived, the spirit came to that place, / [bringing] blooming tree [branches], cool-watered, a charming water vessel,
joined with curd-rice, and accompanied by a dish. / Then, descending, he gave the fine food to the guest at that time.
