By the mere eating there, he attained supreme satisfaction. / Free of thirst and free of fever, he became so in an instant.
And then the spirits arrived; he gave a share in due order from this / curd-rice with drinking water, and the spirits reached supreme satisfaction.
Having gratified the guest and the spirit realm on all sides, / then he himself ate the remainder of the food at ease.
When he had eaten, the fine food and the drinking water vanished. / Then the merchant spoke these words to that lord of spirits:
'This seems to me a great wonder in this forest. / And from where was supreme food and drink obtained by you?
With so little food, indeed, you satisfied even these many. / But how are these fleshless, with ruptured bellies?
And how have you made an abode in this exceedingly dreadful forest? / Resolve this doubt of mine; my curiosity is supreme.'
Thus addressed by the merchant, the spirit spoke the words: / 'Formerly, when I was attached to trade in my past life, O sinless one,
in the whole town, there was indeed no other evil-minded person like me. / Out of greed for wealth, alms were never given by me then to anyone.
And then I had a friend, a virtuous brāhmaṇa. / Then, at the conjunction of Śravaṇadvādaśī in the month of Bhādrapada,
he once went with me to the river named Tāpī, / where her holy confluence was with the Candrabhāgā.
The Candrabhāgā is the daughter of the Moon, and the Tāpī is the daughter of the Sun. / Into their cold and warm waters, that twice-born entered.
On the conjunction of the Śravaṇadvādaśī, men who had fasted / gave to a twice-born a water vessel with the water of the Candrabhāgā,
along with curd-rice, accompanied by full dishes, / an umbrella, a pair of sandals, cloth, and likewise an image of Hari.
he gave [it] to the foremost brāhmaṇas before Hara, O highly intelligent one. / For the sake of preserving wealth, during the vow on its bank, by me
a single charming water-jar was given while fasting. / Having done that, I reached home; then, after some time,
I met with death and became a ghost on account of unbelief / in this dreadful forest, just like a brood of serpents.
At the conjunction of Śravaṇā and the twelfth lunar day, that water-jar was offered by me; / and that very [jar] is obtained day after day at midday.
All these sinners who had the nature of brāhmaṇas have become ghosts; / some had gone after other men's wives, and those who were intent on betraying their masters
were born here, indeed, as humans in the form of spirits and ghosts. / In this desert region they have become my friends.
The Blessed One, Viṣṇu, the eternal Supreme Self, is imperishable; / whatever is given intending him is proclaimed to be imperishable.
And though satisfied again and again with imperishable food, / the condition of being a ghost and weakness never leave [them].
Having honored you, a guest who has arrived, with food, / I shall be released from the ghost-state and go to the supreme state.
Bereft of me, however, in this exceedingly terrible forest, / these will experience terrible torment born of the womb of their past actions.
Therefore, O fortunate one, out of a desire to show grace to me, / take down the names and gotras of each of them, written down.
And indeed, in your armpit is an auspicious casket. / Then, having reached the Himavat, you will find a treasure there.
Having gone from there to Gayāśīrṣa, perform a śrāddha, O highly intelligent one.” / Having thus instructed the merchant at ease, that ghost
then dismissed him. He, full of eagerness, departed. / Having reached home, he subsequently set out for the Himālaya.
Having taken the treasure seen there, he returned; / then, taking a sixth part, he went from there to Gayāśīrṣa.
Having gone there to Gayā, that highly intelligent man performed a śrāddha, / a śrāddha properly according to rule for the ghosts, as had been designated.
Taking the names and gotras of each one, he offered the rice-ball. / On whichever day the merchant performed the śrāddha for someone,
that very one then showed his own form to him in a dream / and said: “O fortunate one, O sinless one! By your grace,
the ghost-state has been abandoned by me, and I have attained the supreme state.” / Having performed thus according to rule at Gayāśīrṣa, the noble-minded one
subsequently went to his own home, meditating on Viṣṇu again and again. / When the month of Bhādrapada arrived, during the bright fortnight, the wise man,
at the conjunction of Śravaṇā and the twelfth lunar day, went again to the confluence of rivers, / that one of great intellect, equipped with all paraphernalia.
Having bathed at the confluence of rivers, he fasted on that twelfth lunar day; / and having bathed and made gifts there, having worshiped Janārdana,
thereupon he presented gifts to the brāhmaṇa, / in accordance with the rule spoken of in the treatises, he too being devoted with a focused mind.
The wise merchant then returned. / And year after year, when the month of Bhādrapada arrived,
at the conjunction of Śravaṇā and the twelfth lunar day, at the confluence of rivers, / he indeed performed everything promptly, intending Viṣṇu.
And after a very long time he met with death / and attained the supreme abode, hard to attain by all mortals.
Even today he plays in Vaikuṇṭha, attended by the messengers of Viṣṇu. / Perform thus, O brāhmaṇa, the vow of Śravaṇā-dvādaśī,
which bestows all good fortune in this world and the next, / produces good intellect, and supremely removes all sins.
Whoever performs such a vow at the conjunction of Śravaṇā and the twelfth lunar day / goes to the world of Viṣṇu by the power of this vow.

6.70.m: Nārada said: / “O God of gods, Lord of the world, bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation, / speak, O best of the gods, [of that] by which one sees no sorrow.”
Maheśa said: / “Listen, O brāhmaṇa: I shall declare the auspicious three-night [vow] of the river, / observed by which hell does not happen to mortals.
Having obtained unequaled longevity, health, good fortune, happiness, and prosperity, / and imperishable offspring, one is honored in heaven.
When the month of Āṣāḍha arrives, [a river] is filled with a flood of river-water; / she is renowned in the Purāṇa as an abode of water constantly.
When it is filled by the dense clouds of the rainy season, that [river] is to be approached with a vow; / or when the river is filled with full streams of water,
then the vow spanning three nights is to be performed with diligence, intending [the river]. / Undertaken on the first lunar day according to wish, the viewing lasts three days.
The flood of the river, as it is found, of the water at the bank, [is to be brought] by women, / or taking that water into a black jar, one should carry it home.
The wise person should bathe in the morning in the river, and going, should worship it. / For a fast of three nights, to the extent of one's ability, O twice-born,
or if unable, one should fast with a single meal. / One should offer an unbroken lamp and worship in the morning and evening,
invoking the great river and also Varuṇa by name, / and installing Keśava who lies upon the waters at the root of the water:
‘Homage to the goddess, to the Gaṅgā, to the Gautamī, and to the river; / to the Sindhu, and also to the Kāverī and the Sarasvatī, homage to you!
To the Tāpī, the Payoṣṇī, the Pūrṇā, and to the one giving delight to Mahendra, / to the Kāśyapī, to the Gaṇḍakī, and to the river Sindhu, homage, homage!
Homage to you, O Varuṇa, who dwell in the waters, dear to Hari! / O lord of aquatic creatures, lord of waters, always grant me auspiciousness!
Accept the guest-water offered by me, and grant me my desired fruit.’ / With pumpkins, coconuts, and auspicious seasonal fruits,
one should prepare a food offering cooked in ghee for the river. / ‘Homage to you, Keśava, Infinite One, who lie upon the waters, homage to you!
Protect me, O Lord, Govinda, be a giver of boons.’ / In this manner worship is to be performed at the proper time in due order,
with prayer and with articles of worship, pure in the rule of three nights. / Having worshiped at the breaking of the fast, one should attend to the water-vessel,
with fruits and flowers, O wise one, by women, children, and men too, / accompanied by singing and instrumental music, overflowing with jars of river water.
Placing it in water after water, one should worship it with fruits and flowers, / with various kinds of grain, and also with throwing water.
With laughter, songs, and dances, having returned home with diligence, / one should worship bamboo vessels filled with the seven grains.
One should fill seven, five, or three, according to one's capacity. / And for three nights one should not drink river water, rejoicing in one's welfare.
At the breaking of the fast, sacrificial food is taken, or it becomes otherwise; / once bathing and worship have been performed, river water is not to be used [for drinking].
One should cause three kinds of pure, edible food to be given, / and exactly seven bamboo vessels and seven water-jars.
One should eat sacrificial food devoid of pungent, sour, and sweet flavors; / and one should diligently avoid black-gram dishes and food ground on stone.
In this way, one should perform this vow for three years, O best of the twice-born. / Having thus completed three years, one should perform its concluding rite.
One should give a black cow, a black cloth, and sesame seeds, O Nārada; / having clothed a married couple, [one should also give] gold according to one's means.
And one should make a golden Varuṇa in the form of a river, O Nārada, / and [prepare] a mandala dedicated to Varuṇa, or a sarvatobhadra [mandala].
Having installed a water jar there, consecrated with offerings, / and worshipped it according to rule with devotion, one should then present it to a brāhmaṇa.
One should feed brāhmaṇas according to one's ability, in proportion to one's wealth, / and [give gifts] to a preceptor who is well-conducted and devoted to all scriptures.
When this is done, O wise one, then the vow becomes complete; / good fortune, happiness, prosperity, and imperishable progeny will ensue.
One does not fall into misfortune and is honored in heaven for a long time. / It was practiced by the wives of gods and the wives of sages,
and this vow was performed in the past by the wives of Nāgas and Siddhas— / this matchless Nadītrirātra vow. What else do you wish to hear? / One always certainly obtains good fortune and progeny.
